metadata.title: When to Keep Spare Servers
metadata.project: Predictive Autoscaling with Reinforcement Learning (Humanitarians AI RL Environments)
metadata.audience: Students and practitioners learning when AI and automation help, and when they do not
metadata.greeting_note: HAI short-form hello lexicon: Italian 'Ciao'. The greeting addresses the person typing (Laksh).
metadata.source_commit_subject: Add Huawei multi-week traces and a PPO agent that sets HPA's target
metadata.source_data: Azure Functions Trace 2019 (Shahrad et al., USENIX ATC 2020), CC-BY 4.0; Huawei Cloud traces 2023 (Joosen et al., ACM SoCC 2023), CC BY 4.0

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW: composer, the ask lands answered. Required fellows intro line first, then the AI-voice disclosure.
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Laksh, and this video is about teaching the Kubernetes autoscaler when to keep spare servers. You hear an AI voice; the project is my own work, built with help from Claude Code.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer: the ask and three results

show.event: greeting and the ask type into the composer
running indicator, then three result lines land

props.command: let PPO pick HPA's target utilization every minute, and test it against HPA at the same cost
output: beats HPA in 53 of 60 runs at the same cost
Huawei held-out: 15% to 57% fewer late requests
Azure held-out apps: only 8 of 15 runs

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW: the hesitant writer types the common framing (set the target once) and corrects it to this reel's claim (every minute).
beats.narration_text: Tune the autoscaler's target every minute, not just once. A learned agent that does this beats a fixed target at the same cost, on most of the tests.

show.event: the writer types 'Tune the autoscaler's target once.'
'once' turns terracotta, is deleted, 'every minute' is typed

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the overview is typed token by token, so mid-beat frames are mostly cream by design.

beats.role_note: one held-out Huawei function (pri-60, day 12), 18:50-19:20, HPA at a 70% target (evidence window); bursts peaking in their first minute (evidence burst_first_minute_pct)
beats.narration_text: HPA, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, adds servers past a target, like seventy percent busy. But most bursts jump within a minute, and new servers take three minutes to boot. Only spare servers help, and a fixed target keeps the same share all day.
beats.new_visual_element: a real burst: requests jump at 19:00, HPA's servers arrive 3 minutes later, late requests in between

show.event: axes; requests and HPA's servers from 18:50
the 19:00 jump draws in; the late area fills
a 3-minute boot bracket
the spare share bracket: about 30% at a 70% target

beats.role_note: train.py Headroom / HEADROOM_TARGETS; env.py observation (window 10, yesterday 10, last week 10, servers, queue, time)
beats.narration_text: So PPO, a reinforcement learning algorithm, picks HPA's target every minute, from forty to ninety percent. It sees recent traffic, yesterday and last week at this time, and its servers. Nobody tells it how to use them.
beats.new_visual_element: the inputs (with the real 10-minute views at 18:58), PPO, six target chips, HPA's rule, servers; the pick moves

show.event: PPO -> six target chips -> HPA rule -> servers
the highlighted chip moves
the four inputs draw in, with their 10-minute views
'nobody tells it how to use them'

beats.role_note: data/*.json sizes and splits, train days (episodes('train', ..., 7)), results/ppo-hpa/*.json (30 runs, 3M steps)
beats.narration_text: It trains on real traffic from Azure and Huawei, with apps and days held out. Thirty runs on Modal, over four hundred fifty-six days, only forty-two from Azure.
beats.new_visual_element: three day bars with held-out apps and unseen days; the 456 training days split; 2 x 5 x 3 = 30 runs

show.event: Azure, Huawei public and Huawei private day bars grow; unseen days outlined
training days bar: 42 Azure of 456
30 runs = 2 x 5 x 3, 3M steps each

beats.role_note: results/stress-hpa.json scenario normal: HPA curve (targets 40-90%) and the 30 PPO runs, four test sets
beats.narration_text: Each dot is one run; the line is HPA at fixed targets. Below the line means fewer late requests at the same cost, and on three of four test sets, every run is below.
beats.new_visual_element: cost against late requests, four test sets: HPA's curve and 30 runs as dots

show.event: four panels and HPA's curves
the 30 runs land as dots per panel

beats.role_note: evidence score: each run vs HPA at its own cost (frontier.rule_late_at, linear between targets)
beats.narration_text: On held-out Huawei functions, that is fifteen to fifty-seven percent fewer late requests. On held-out Azure apps, only eight of fifteen runs win.
beats.new_visual_element: score card: runs better of 15 and the range, both training variants, four test sets

show.event: Huawei rows tick in
the Azure held-out row: 8 and 10 of 15

beats.role_note: results/stress-hpa.json six changed scenarios x 4 test sets x 15 runs, each against HPA under the same change
beats.narration_text: If yesterday or last week misleads, the agent still beats HPA in fifty-eight percent of cases. Trained with misleading history, seventy-six percent.
beats.new_visual_element: the three changes; two bars of cases won out of 360 (58%, 76%); normal history 53 and 55 of 60; worst case 93% and 64%

show.event: history days; yesterday and last week get the three changes
bar: 208 of 360
bar: 273 of 360
normal history and worst case lines

beats.role_note: evidence burstiness (held-out Azure apps vs the median Azure training app), azure_apps_by_penalty, env.py ClusterConfig; README Limits
beats.narration_text: The limits: four of the five held-out Azure apps are two to four times burstier than a typical Azure training app. There, lean agents lose and agents with more spare servers win. And the servers are simulated.
beats.new_visual_element: five burstiness bars against the training median; lean vs spare-keeping runs; the simulated-server facts

show.event: burstiness bars grow; the median line
lowest penalty 0 of 6, highest 6 of 6
simulated servers: 600 requests per minute, 3-minute boot, same cost; HPA in production: CPU, every 15 s

beats.narration_text: Next: more varied traffic and balanced training, real server data to calibrate the simulator, and a test of which history inputs help.

show.event: three steps tick in, in narration order

beats.role_note: recap card; the narration carries the takeaway
beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Keep HPA's rule, let a learned agent pick its target, and judge it at the same cost, on traffic it never saw.

show.event: the artifact card lists five lines

artifactLines: The baseline: HPA with one fixed target.
PPO picks HPA's target every minute.
Better than HPA in 53 of 60 runs, same cost.
When history misleads: 76% of cases won.
Not yet on bursty Azure held-out apps.

beats.role_note: YOUR TURN LAW: one prompt the viewer can paste, read aloud verbatim, then one line on what to look for
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Here is my autoscaler's target utilization and a month of my traffic. Find the hours when a lower target would have saved the most late requests per extra server. If those hours repeat daily, keep spares there.
